Learning Objectives
Define terminology related to strength training.
Recognize the advantages of strength training in young athletes.
Evaluate medical conditions in which strength training is contraindicated.
Determine the appropriate supervision for injury reduction.
Introduction
Strength training, also called resistance training, is an accepted training method in children
and adolescents.

Introduction
Resistance training is the mechanism of using a range of resistive loads (kettlebells, free
weights, machine-based, and resistance bands) to improve strength.2 Strength training is
a safe and effective component of long-term athletic development, encouraging physical
fitness and psychosocial well-being.3 Strength development is multifactorial, influenced
by muscular, neural, mechanical, psychological, and hormonal factors.4
Health Benefits
Improvements in Cardiovascular Health
Reduction of apolipoprotein B, which is involved in deposition of low-density lipoprotein (LDL)
Increase in insulin sensitivity in overweight children and a decrease in fasting insulin levels in
children and adolescents7
Spontaneous daily activity levels of school-aged male hockey athletes and nonathletic
schoolchildren were increased months after completion of a training program compared with
similar population controls who did not participate in the training program.8,9

Improvements in Cardiovascular Health
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:40 AM
AAOS | Strength Training and Conditioning in the Young Athlete
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002091
3/17

Apolipoprotein B is the protein carrier of LDL and carries LDL throughout the
bloodstream. Apolipoprotein B and LDL are the important causal agents of
atherosclerotic disease.5 A statistically significant decrease in apolipoprotein B levels
were found in overweight adolescents involved in a 4-week program of combined
aerobic and resistance training compared with adolescents not in a program.6
Improvements in Bone Health
Improvements in bone health include an increase in bone mineral density and improved
cardiometabolic health.10, 11
Increasing bone strength index and mineral content may lead to a decrease in the number of
injuries during sport-specific practice and competition.12
Improvements in Neuromuscular Control
Prepubertal children gain strength via neuromuscular pathways, specifically recruiting an
increased number of motor neurons to generate muscle contraction. This is in direct contrast
to post-pubertal adolescents, who gain muscle strength primarily via muscular hypertrophy.13
A decrease in electromechanical delay also occurs, which is the time it takes muscles to
contract after neuronal signaling because of increased tendon stiffness.12 This allows for the
dissipation of impact forces while maintaining proper limb alignment.14

Improvements in Neuromuscular Control
An increase in tendon robustness contributes to muscle hypertrophy during puberty.
With increased strength, an increase in the rate of force development occurs, which is
the rate an amount of force can be exerted by a muscle group.12 Performance
measurements of vertical jumps, countermovement jumps, and sprint times provide
evidence that overall strength increases.2 Greater strength allows for improved ability to
use the stretch shortening cycle in managing ground reaction forces.15

Improved Physical Literacy
Improved physical literacy has been linked to higher resilience.16
Improvements in strength allow for fundamental movement skill development and
preparation to learn more complex movements and sport-specific skills.17,18
In adolescents who are overweight or obese, having improved physical literacy increases
confidence in resistance training and self-esteem, which is an overall positive effect on
psychological well-being.19
Injury Mitigation
Reduction in the risk of noncontact anterior cruciate ligament tears in female and male soccer
players20
Reduction of knee injuries in female athletes playing volleyball, basketball, and handball using
neuromuscular training programs21,22
Reduction in occurrence of tennis elbow and swimmer shoulder23,24
Reduction in medial elbow injury in children aged 8 to 11 years and adolescent baseball
players who underwent a program of strengthening and stretching exercises compared with
players who did not25
Reduction in hamstring injuries in collegiate-level sprinters with a strength-training program
incorporating agility and flexibility training26
Increased accessory muscle strength and tendon strength through resistance training may
help prevent injuries in sport-specific practice and competition.12
Areas of Caution
Medical Conditions That May Restrict Participation
Athletes with hypertension should be evaluated before participation in strength training,
especially with free weights, because systolic and diastolic blood pressures rise considerably
during these maneuvers.
Athletes with seizure disorders may require modifications to exercises to reduce risk of injury
should a seizure occur, but otherwise can participate freely in resistance training if seizures
are controlled.29

If an athlete has severe seizures, he or she should consider modifying the equipment used (eg,
substituting stationary machine-based or seated equipment for free weights or a treadmill) to
prevent injury if a seizure occurs.

Medical Conditions That May Restrict Participation
Athletes who have prehypertension and stage 1 hypertension without evidence of end-
organ damage should not be limited in sports activity.27 Athletes with stage 2
hypertension or signs of end-organ damage should be restricted from high static sports
(eg, boxing, weightlifting, wrestling) until blood pressure is controlled.27 In athletes with
prehypertension that is sustained after lifestyle modifications, an echocardiogram
should be obtained to evaluate for left ventricular hypertrophy.27 According to the 2017
American Academy of Pediatrics Clinical Practice Guideline for Screening and
Management of High Blood Pressure in Children and Adolescents, hypertension is
defined as follows.28 In children aged 1 to 13 years: elevated blood pressure is systolic
and diastolic blood pressure greater or equal to the ninetieth and less than the ninety-
fifth percentile; stage 1 hypertension is systolic blood pressure greater or equal to the
ninety-fifth percentile to less than the ninety-fifth percentile +12 mm Hg; and stage 2
hypertension is systolic blood pressure greater or equal to the ninety-fifth percentile +
12 mm Hg. In patients older than 13 years: elevated blood pressure is systolic blood
pressure 120 to 129 mm Hg and diastolic blood pressure is less than 80 mm Hg; stage 1
hypertension is 130/80 mm Hg to 139/89 mm Hg; and stage 2 hypertension is greater or
equal to 140/90 mm Hg.
Absolute Contraindications to Resistance Training
The following conditions are absolute contraindications to resistance training because the
underlying pathology may lead to serious harm or death in athletes.
Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
In young, competitive athletes, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the most common cause of
sudden cardiac death.30 The cause of death is most likely related to the development of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:40 AM
AAOS | Strength Training and Conditioning in the Young Athlete
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002091
6/17

ventricular tachycardia/ventricular fibrillation.30 The findings can be elicited on physical
examination upon auscultation of a systolic ejection crescendo-decrescendo murmur along
the left sternal border. The murmur is louder with decreased preload (Valsalva maneuver,
diuretics, standing) and softer with increased preload (squatting) or increased afterload
(handgrip).31
Pulmonary Hypertension
Pulmonary hypertension as a primary etiology or secondary to cardiac valvular disease places
athletes at risk for symptoms, including arrhythmias, syncope, chest pain, or sudden death.32
Marfan Syndrome
Marfan syndrome and other related aortic diseases place athletes at risk of aortic dissection.33
Anthracycline Chemotherapy
Exposure to anthracycline chemotherapy may lead to abnormal cardiac function secondary to
the cardiotoxicity of the drugs, placing athletes at increased risk of cardiac decompensation.34
Guidance for recommended restrictions for athletes with cardiovascular disease can be found
in a 2015 publication released by the American Heart Association and the American College of
Cardiology that provides updated recommendations on eligibility and restriction criteria for
young, competitive athletes with underlying cardiovascular abnormalities35 (Resource 1).
Prior to this document, three Bethesda Conferences produced publications with
recommendations on this topic.
Risks Unique to the Pediatric Population
With maturing skeletal systems, young athletes are at increased risk of damage to the
apophyseal and epiphyseal areas when performing explosive lifts with improper form.
The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that young athletes rest 1 to 2 days per
week for physical and mental recovery, which also should include the athlete’s other sport
training requirements as well.

Risks Unique to the Pediatric Population
Injuries associated with unsupervised training include wrist fractures (bilateral and
unilateral) while performing overhead presses at a home gym and bench presses during
unsupervised weight training.36,37 The most vulnerable body areas for injury vary
depending on patient age. In children aged 8 to 13 years, more than 60% of injuries
occur in the hands and feet, usually from pinching, dropping weights, or tripping over
equipment. These accidents likely occur because children do not receive proper
supervision.38 Most injuries in the younger age group are accidental.39 Conversely, in
older athletes, 42% of injuries occur in the trunk37 (Figure 1). Children and adolescents
should not participate in resistance training for competition (eg, powerlifting,
weightlifting, bodybuilding) because this requires maximal lifts at too young an age,
which may be dangerous.12

youngest age categories. Note that the small prevalence of leg injuries in the 8- to 13-
year category is not validated and should be interpreted with caution. (Reproduced with
permission from Myer GD, Quatman CE, Khoury J, Wall EJ, Hewett TE: Youth versus adult

Chronic Overuse Injuries Requiring Medical Attention
Spondylolysis
Stress fracture of the pars interarticularis of the vertebra, usually the fourth or fifth lumbar
vertebra unilaterally or bilaterally39 Common in strength sports because of increased loads
placed on the axial spine.40
Spondylolisthesis
Unmanaged spondylolysis that leads to separation of the pars interarticularis fracture and the
injured vertebra slipping forward39
Osteolysis of Distal Clavicle
Repetitive stress and microfractures leading to osteopenia
Most commonly observed among weightlifters, and patients typically present with anterior
shoulder pain and tenderness at the acromioclavicular joint.41, 42
Radiographs demonstrate loss of subchondral bone in the distal clavicle and subchondral
bone cystic changes.41, 42
Several underlying medical causes should be considered and appropriately ruled out, including
hyperparathyroidism and rheumatoid arthritis.
Hyperparathyroidism-related changes typically present as bilateral erosions caused by
subchondral bone resorption.
Rheumatoid arthritis–related changes typically present as bilateral erosions with soft-tissue
swelling, erosion of the outer third of the clavicle, and subchondral osteoporosis.
Tendinopathy
Chronic tendon injury caused by overload
Because of the varied time course of adaptation to mechanical loading and mechanical
stimulation between muscle and tendon, a possible imbalance of muscle strength and tendon

stiffness can occur.43
Maturation and mechanical loading, specifically athletes performing a high volume of jumps
(eg, in basketball or volleyball), are the greatest risks.43
Tendon tissue responds best to specific contraction intensity, duration, and joint angles.43
Stress Fractures
Chronic injuries that result from repetitive loads at a site.40
If stress fractures are not managed appropriately, they can progress to overt fractures.
Acute Injuries
Disk herniations
Joint dislocations, which usually result from losing control of the weight in a vulnerable
position for injury40
Tendon ruptures from overloading the tensile strength of the tendon rather than from
inappropriate movement of the joint40
Fractures
Strength Training Regimen
Modalities of Resistance
Body weight, free weights, medicine balls, kettlebells, elastic bands, weight machines, and
plyometrics
Systematic, individualized progression and exposure to a varied range of movements
encourages positive health, enjoyment, and better performance.3
Ensure proper technique, balance, and motor control before introducing high-reaction
forces.15
Appropriate Supervision
A certified coach should be present at all training sessions. Recommendations of approved
certifications include:2 certified strength and conditioning specialist through the National
Strength and Conditioning Association, accredited strength and conditioning coach through

the United Kingdom Strength and Conditioning Association, and USA weightlifting coach
through USA Weightlifting.
Limit the number of athletes based on athlete training level, athlete age, and coach experience
to allow for adequate supervision.
With appropriate supervision and gradual progression of exercise, strength gains can occur
without an increased risk of injury.
An evaluation of resistance training injuries in high school football players revealed that only
36% of training sessions were appropriately supervised.
Strength Training Specific Recommendations
Can initiate strength training in children aged 5 to 7-years because this the time children
become involved in athletics and have appropriate gross motor development to perform some
of the exercises (eg, fundamental movement patterns, such as squatting, lunging, bracing,
crawling, pressing, and climbing)44
Training prescription should consider biologic age and psychosocial maturity level.47
Start with proper technique and slowly add weight, ensuring proper technique is maintained.
Account for time spent strength training as part of total training time to reduce the risk of
overuse injuries. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that the number of hours
per week of exercise do not exceed a child’s age in years.

Strength Training Specific Recommendations
These skills are supported by strength training and are important for physical, social,
and cognitive development. They also help establish a foundation for an active
lifestyle.45 Participants should be able to accept instruction, understand safety protocols,
and have the requisite capacity for posture and motor control.46
Peak height velocity describes the period in which an adolescent’s rate of growth is the
fastest. Typically, the onset of the adolescent growth spurt coincides with the onset of
puberty and occurs in girls aged approximately 11 years and in boys aged approximately
13 years; however, this will vary considerably among individuals. This rapid period of
growth creates biomechanical changes and deficits that leave a young athlete at greater

11/17

risk of injury.47 Increasing strength and improving movement ability is the best strategy
for reducing injury risk in sports activity.47 Skeletal muscle hypertrophy and bone
maturation are improved because of increased concentration of anabolic hormones (eg,
estrogen, testosterone, insulin-like growth factor-1, and growth hormone).48
Comprehensive positive effects in health and performance not only result from sports
participation but also a structured resistance training program.49
The amount of exercise, level of intensity, and amount of weight should be gradually
increased. The exact training regimen, including types of exercises, amount of weight,
and frequency, depends on an athlete’s individual resistance training skill competency. A
proper resistance training regimen should include three critical aspects: education
regarding proper lifting form, adequate supervision, and effectively scaled lifting.12
Recent studies show that a minimum duration training program of 8 weeks with a
frequency of two to three times per week may lead to improved strength; however, a
program of more than 23 weeks is most effective. For increased tendon stiffness,
exposure to an intensity of 85% to 90% isometric voluntary maximum contraction,
lasting at least 3 seconds and through a range of strain that maximizes force generation
(eg, between 60° and 100° of knee flexion in a parallel squat; 0° = full extension) is
recommended.43
Summary/Outcomes
Resistance training involves the use of resistive forces to increase strength.
In children and adolescent athletes, multiple health and sport benefits exist, including
improvements in cardiovascular health and overall well-being, motor skill acquisition, reduced
injury risk, and improved athletic performance.12
Appropriate supervision decreases the risk of preventable injuries.
For children and adolescents with certain medical conditions, strength training should be
avoided or modified. These include hypertension, Marfan syndrome, pulmonary hypertension,
seizures, exposure to anthracycline chemotherapy, and other cardiac pathologies.
